newsitem.title: ITALY: Romantic intellectual in vogue for man about Milan.
newsitem.headline: Romantic intellectual in vogue for man about Milan.

text.p: Romance and intellectualism provided the muse for the 1997/98 autumn/winter menswear designs of Italian stylists Gianfranco Ferre and Krizia at the Milan ready to wear fashion shows on Monday.
High-fastening jackets, minimalist collars and autumnal browns, moss greens and sombre greys coloured both collections.
While Krizia delved into late nineteenth century nostalgia, Ferre drew on images of wordsmiths such as Irish playwright Samuel Beckett.
"These are examples of men I wanted my people to be surrounded by -- severe and eccentric," Ferre told Reuters.

"This collection has a pure touch of romance. It's not just done with frills and double collars but a very refined choice of material and of spirit," he said, speaking after his show. "This is a very tailored man but at the same time very modern."
Suits were double breasted with four and six buttons in grey or black, chalk striped with narrow, tapered pants and turn-ups.
Trench coats were broad but soft shouldered while fabrics and colours included herringbone, checks and camel.
Ferre produced a Norfolk jacket with four pockets belted at the front and a set of dresscoats, cut close at the top and sweeping down to the ankle with one deep vent up the back.
Velvet jackets in bottle green, black blue and burgundy, some with Nehru collars, featured for evening, with velvet pants trimmed at the side by a dark military style stripe.
Krizia pulled starched white cuffs out from under her jacket sleeves, leaving them unfastened over black leather gloves in her collection of "new romanticism" earlier on Monday.

The stylist, whose real name is Mariuccia Mandelli, cited the era of U.S. impressionist artist John Singer Sargent and said turn-ups and a slim profile with shoulders in proportion caught "the essence of the silhouette of Krizia's man of today."
Shirt collars were small and neat, sometimes nonexistent and often covered by a woollen scarf tucked under jacket lapels.

Suit jackets were fastened high up the breast bone with three or four buttons for single breasts and six or eight for double breasts while coat collars fell deep and round over secured top buttons to give a neat, contained look.

Krizia gave jackets three pockets, two on either hip and one buttoned but flapless at the breast, while coat and jacket backs had a button at either kidney, accentuating the high slim waist and a slight flare over the hips.
Trousers were straight or narrow legged, stopping above chunky winter sandals and thick, heavy knit woollen socks.

Outdoorwear included thigh-length reefers and imposing greatcoats in chocolate brown, mossy green and stone while for evening a four-button single breasted suit in black velvet with protruding white shirt cuffs captured the collection's mood.

A more saucy look came from the slender-hipped Sicilian profiles cast by Domenico Dolce and Stefano Gabbana's designs, with trousers cut low over the hip and narrow down the leg with deep turn-ups over the ankle.
Dolce & Gabbana abandoned ties, presenting close-cut two and three-piece chalk striped suits with white shirts buttoned up to a round collarless neck or with matching turtleneck tops.
